1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: The point of 3.c3: White challenges e5 at once and ignores the loose pawn on e4, so Black chooses which central pawn to take. Either way White aims to win the pawn back with gain of time, in games that run from quiet to wild.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Defends e4 with a modest pawn but gives up the quick d4 push that made 3.c3 worthwhile. The c3 pawn looks misplaced and the light-squared bishop is hemmed in behind the pawns, so Black takes the centre at once.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3.name: Ponziani Opening: Jaenisch Counterattack

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Bc4.strategy: Eyes f7 but leaves the pawn on e4 undefended. Black simply takes it, and with c3 occupied White has nothing concrete in return. The best White can do is trade bishop for knight and win the pawn back, when Black still has the easier game.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Bc4.name: Ponziani Opening: Neumann Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Bc4.background: Jules Arnous de Rivière played it against Gustav Neumann in 1864, and databases use both names for it. Radjabov played it against Anand in 2009, reaching it by the Italian Game move order, and Anand declined the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 d5.name: Ponziani Opening: Jaenisch Counterattack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and attacks e4 a second time, so White needs another defender. White has shut in its own bishop behind the pawns and the c3 pawn looks out of place, while Black develops comfortably.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4.strategy: Grabs the loose pawn and puts the knight on a square from which it eyes f2. A bishop on c5 would attack that pawn twice, which is why White cannot simply recapture on e5. The main line, with White fighting to win the pawn back safely.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 d5 5.Nbd.name: Ponziani Opening: Jaenisch Counterattack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 d5 5.Nbd.strategy: The solid reply: it adds a second guard to e4 and develops the knight to d2, the natural square now that c3 is taken. White keeps a compact pawn centre and plays slowly, while Black has the freer game and must find a plan.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 5.d.strategy: Kicks the knight from c6 so that e5 loses its defender and White can win the pawn back. The price is control of c5: the pawn on d4 no longer guards it, so Black may answer with a sharp sacrifice. The traditional main line.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 5.d.name: Ponziani Opening: Vukovic Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 5.d.background: Ernst Falkbeer played 5...Bc5 in 1855, and Chigorin first tried the improvement 6...Bxf2+ against Eugen von Schmidt in St Petersburg in 1879. For a century the gambit was thought refuted; 7...Bb6 was revived only in the 2000s. It is also called the Fraser Defence.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 5.d.strategy: Instead of saving the knight, Black lines up bishop and knight on f2 and sacrifices a piece for pawns and an exposed white king. Very sharp, with exact play needed from both sides and good practical results, but Black has to prove the compensation.
